solutions.latex: Exact area under the curve: $$\text{Area}=\int_0^3 x^3-3x^2+3x+4\,dx=\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-x^3+\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+4x\right]_0^3=\dfrac{75}{4}\text{ or }18.75$$ Estimate of the area under the curve using two applications of the trapezoidal rule: $$\text{Area}\approx\dfrac{1.5}{2}[4+2\times 5.125+13]\approx 20.4375$$ $$20.4375-18.75=1.6875$$ Hence the trapezoidal rule overestimates the exact area under the curve by 1.6875 square units.

solutions.latex: Total distance travelled may be modelled as the limiting sum of a geometric series, since $0<r<1$. $$S_\infty=H+2(h_1+h_2+h_3+\cdots)=H+2\left(\dfrac{\frac{qH}{100}}{1-\frac{q}{100}}\right)$$ $$=H+\dfrac{2qH}{100-q}\rightarrow=\dfrac{H(100-q)}{100-q}+\dfrac{2qH}{100-q}$$ $$=\dfrac{100H-qH+2qH}{100-q}\rightarrow=\dfrac{100H+qH}{100-q}=\dfrac{H(100+q)}{100-q}$$

solutions.latex: Maximise the volume by maximising the area of the cross-section, since the depth is constant. Let $A$ be the area of the cross-section of the tent. $$A=5xy+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 5x\times h=5xy+\dfrac{5xh}{2}$$ From parts (a) and (b): $$A=5x(10-4x)+\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}x^2}{4}=50x-20x^2+\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}x^2}{4}=50x-\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)x^2$$ Determine stationary point and its nature: $$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=50-2\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)x$$ $$50-2\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)x=0$$ $$\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)x=25$$ $$x=25\div\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)=2.05$$ $$\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2}=-2\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)=-24.387\ldots<0$$ Hence maximum volume at $x=2.05$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 3: Provides correct solution; 2: Finds stationary point, or equivalent merit; 1: Finds correct expression for surface area of tent, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: Find the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$ by equating $y=x^3-2x$ with $y=x^2$. $$x^3-2x=x^2$$ $$x^3-x^2-2x=0$$ $$x(x^2-x-2)=0$$ $$x(x+1)(x-2)=0$$ hence the $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $-1$ and the $x$-coordinate of $B$ is 2. Area between the two curves is given by $$\text{Area}=\left|\int_{-1}^{0}x^3-x^2-2x\,dx\right|+\left|\int_0^2 x^3-x^2-2x\,dx\right|$$ $$=\left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_{-1}^{0}\right|+\left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_0^2\right|$$ $$=\left|\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{3}-1\right|+\left|4-\dfrac{8}{3}-4\right|=\dfrac{5}{12}+\dfrac{8}{3}=\dfrac{37}{12}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 4: Provides correct solution; 3: Correctly sets up a sum of two integrals, including correct bounds for each integral, and attempts to find the area between the two curves, or equivalent merit; 2: Finds the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$, or equivalent merit; 1: Attempts to find the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$ by equating the functions, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\text{LHS}=\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\cos(90^\circ-\theta)}(1+\tan^2\theta)+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}[1+\tan^2(90^\circ-\theta)]$$ $$=\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\times\sec^2\theta+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}(1+\cot^2\theta)$$ $$=\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\times\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta}+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\times\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta$$ $$=\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\times\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta}+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta}$$ $$=\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}+\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}$$ $$=2\operatorname{cosec}\theta\sec\theta=\text{RHS}$$

solutions.latex: Divide the numerator and denominator of the integrand by $x^2$ such that: $$\int\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\,dx=\int\dfrac{\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}}{\frac{x\ln x}{x^2}}\,dx=\int\dfrac{\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}}{\frac{\ln x}{x}}\,dx$$ Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$ and $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln x+c$: $$\int\dfrac{\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}}{\frac{\ln x}{x}}\,dx\text{ is in the form }\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx$$ Hence, $$\int\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\,dx=\ln\left|\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right|+c=\ln|\ln x|-\ln|x|+c$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 3: Provides correct solution; 2: Makes substantial progress toward correct solution, such as recognising that the integral is in the form $\int\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ and hence will result in a log function by using the fact that $\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{\ln x}{x}\right)=\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$, or equivalent merit; 1: Divides numerator and denominator by $x^2$, or equivalent merit
